definition: A difference a writer draws attention to by putting things side by side.
example: The contrast between the warm party and the cold office is clear.

definition: The words characters say to one another.
example: We hear Fred invite Scrooge to dinner through their dialogue.

definition: To repeat an earlier word, image or idea in a way that gives it fresh meaning.
example: The ghost’s words echo what Scrooge said earlier.

definition: The voice that tells a story.
example: The narrator tells us that Marley is dead.

definition: The deliberate use of a word, sound or pattern more than once.
example: Saying “Good afternoon!” again and again is repetition.

definition: A comparison that uses “like” or “as”.
example: “Solitary as an oyster” is a simile.

definition: The attitude or feeling conveyed by a speaker’s or writer’s choice of words.
example: Fred speaks to his uncle in a friendly tone.

definition: An office worker who keeps records, writes letters or manages accounts.
example: Bob works as a clerk in Scrooge’s office.

definition: Cold, bare or without much hope.
example: The empty schoolroom feels cold and bleak.

definition: Careful about what one says or does because something might go wrong.
example: Bob is cautious about asking for Christmas Day off.

definition: Strange in a way that makes a familiar place or object feel unsettling.
example: Marley’s face in the door knocker gives Scrooge an eerie feeling.

definition: Willing to give time, money or care freely.
example: Scrooge is generous when he buys the Cratchits a turkey.

definition: Separated from other people or lacking contact with them.
example: Eating alone on Christmas Eve shows how isolated Scrooge is.

definition: The ways a writer builds a picture of what a character is like.
example: Dickens begins Bob’s characterisation with a small action. Warming himself at a candle shows how little power he has in the office.

definition: An idea or feeling a word brings to mind beyond its literal meaning.
example: The connotation of worship in Belle’s word “idol” suggests that money now commands the devotion Scrooge once gave her.

definition: To describe or treat people as though their individual lives do not matter.
example: Scrooge’s talk of a surplus population works to dehumanise people by reducing them to a number.

definition: A way of speaking or writing that turns directly to the listener or reader.
example: The narrator’s direct address in the opening makes the reader feel like someone being told a ghost story by the fire.

definition: To give an idea extra weight or draw particular attention to it.
example: Tiny Tim’s carefully preserved crutch and his empty seat emphasise his absence from the family.

definition: To bring a feeling, memory or image to mind.
example: The fiddle music and stamping feet at Fezziwig’s party evoke the pleasure of being swept into a dance.

definition: To give an early hint of something that happens later.
example: Marley’s chain serves to foreshadow the reckoning that Scrooge faces when he sees his own grave.

definition: Language that helps a reader picture something or experience it through the senses.
example: The heat, steam and smells in the Cratchits’ kitchen create imagery that makes the reader feel like another guest at dinner.

definition: To suggest something without saying it directly.
example: When Scrooge keeps the coal-box in his own room, the scene lets Dickens imply that even Bob’s warmth is under his employer’s control.

definition: A gap between what is said or expected and what is actually true or happens.
example: There is irony in Bob expecting punishment for arriving late on the very morning Scrooge intends to raise his pay.

definition: A description that speaks of one thing as though it were another.
example: The metaphor of cold inside Scrooge turns his lack of human warmth into something that seems to freeze his very features.

definition: Giving a human action or quality to something that is not human.
example: The personification of the weather makes the rain seem generous beside Scrooge, who will give nothing away.

definition: The process of making amends for past wrongs and changing the way one lives.
example: Scrooge’s redemption becomes convincing when he raises Bob’s pay, because Bob will feel the benefit long after Christmas Day.

definition: To stand for an idea beyond the thing itself.
example: Tiny Tim’s empty seat can symbolise the place a child holds in family life.

definition: To make an idea or claim seem less convincing.
example: The Cratchits’ careful preparations undermine Scrooge’s assumption that poor people are idle.

definition: A woman paid to do cleaning jobs, often by the day.
example: The charwoman claims the first turn at Old Joe’s, as if selling a dead man’s belongings were an ordinary piece of business.

definition: In this setting, a long scarf worn for warmth.
example: Bob has to wear his comforter indoors, a detail that makes Scrooge’s control of the coal feel especially mean.

definition: A business office where money, accounts and correspondence are handled.
example: Scrooge leaves the counting-house door open so he can watch Bob, making the office feel more like a place of surveillance than trust.

definition: A thin food made by cooking grain, often oats, in water or milk.
example: Scrooge’s solitary bowl of gruel makes a quiet contrast with the meals that bring people together elsewhere in the story.

definition: A sham or deception, also used to dismiss something as insincere nonsense.
example: Calling Christmas a humbug tells us that Scrooge distrusts the goodwill Fred offers him.

definition: A woman who earned money by washing clothes and household linen.
example: At Old Joe’s, the laundress can turn a dead man’s linen into cash, showing what his possessions are worth when affection is absent.

definition: A book in which a business records money paid and received.
example: A ledger normally records what someone owes in money, but the ledgers in Marley’s chain suggest a different kind of debt.

definition: A unit of British money worth twelve old pence, with twenty shillings to a pound.
example: Bob supports his family on a wage counted out in the shilling, fifteen of them a week, so even a modest Christmas dinner represents a considerable expense.

definition: A person whose work is to arrange funerals and care for the dead.
example: The undertaker signs the record of Marley’s burial, giving the narrator a practical reason to insist that Marley really is dead.

definition: In the sense used for the child’s name, a severe lack of basic necessities.
example: By naming the girl Want, Dickens gives hunger and material need the face of a child.

definition: An institution where people in poverty received food and shelter under strict rules, with work required of those able to do it.
example: Scrooge treats the workhouse as an answer to hunger, but the charity collector tells him that some people would sooner die than go there.

definition: Present in large amounts, with plenty to spare.
example: The food heaped around the Ghost of Christmas Present is so abundant that the reader has to ask why anyone in the city goes hungry.

definition: Feeling cut off from other people or from a group.
example: The schoolboy left behind at Christmas looks painfully alienated once we see how eagerly the other boys set off for home.

definition: Wanting to help others and acting on that wish.
example: Fezziwig is a benevolent employer because he spends his own time and money making the apprentices feel welcome.

definition: Showing little concern for the pain or feelings of others.
example: Scrooge’s remark about reducing the population sounds particularly callous once the reader knows a child whose life is at risk.

definition: Shared by a group or done together.
example: The lighthouse keepers toast each other before the older man strikes up a song, making Christmas feel communal even out at sea.

definition: So satisfied with oneself or an arrangement that its faults go unnoticed.
example: Scrooge sounds complacent when he learns that the workhouses are still operating and asks nothing about life inside them.

definition: Empty or lonely in a way that causes sadness.
example: The young Scrooge’s schoolroom feels desolate because its one remaining pupil has no one with whom to share the holiday.

definition: Without enough money or resources to meet basic needs.
example: The charity collectors ask for food and warmth for destitute people, bringing the conversation back to what it takes to survive a winter night.

definition: Showing a sense of personal worth that deserves respect.
example: Mrs Cratchit gives the small pudding a dignified entrance, carrying it in with a sprig of holly as though it were a grand centrepiece.

definition: Treating a person or idea as unworthy of serious attention.
example: Scrooge’s repeated farewells are dismissive because each one cuts short Fred’s invitation to talk.

definition: No longer close to someone with whom there is a family or personal connection.
example: Scrooge’s surprise at the welcome he receives from Fred shows how long he has been estranged from his nephew.

definition: So full of energy or joy that it shows in a person’s movements or voice.
example: Scrooge’s exuberant laughter on Christmas morning gives us an audible sign of a change that began in private.

definition: So severe or unwelcoming that people are reluctant to approach.
example: Scrooge cuts such a forbidding figure in the street that even people who need directions leave him alone.

definition: Sad and lonely, especially after being left behind.
example: Seeing his forlorn younger self moves Scrooge to think about the carol singer he sent away.

definition: Careful to make money or supplies go as far as possible.
example: Mrs Cratchit’s ribbons make her old dress festive, showing how a frugal household can still take pleasure in an occasion.

definition: So distorted or unnatural in appearance that it is disturbing.
example: The grotesque appearance of Ignorance and Want makes it difficult for the reader to look away from what neglect has done to them.

definition: Showing no particular interest or concern.
example: The businessmen are so indifferent to the dead man that the possibility of lunch matters more to them than his funeral.

definition: Angry because something seems unfair or insulting.
example: Mrs Cratchit is indignant when Bob praises Scrooge at dinner because she knows whose labour has paid for their meal.

definition: Cheerful and ready to share a joke or a good time.
example: The jovial Ghost of Christmas Present invites Scrooge closer, making this first encounter feel more like a welcome than a haunting.

definition: Giving money and possessions more importance than love or other values.
example: Belle identifies a materialistic turn in Scrooge when she realises that he now measures their future together by its financial risks.

definition: A quiet sadness that tends to linger.
example: There is a melancholy gap between Scrooge’s delight at seeing Fan again and his knowledge that his sister is dead.

definition: Unwilling to spend or share money, even when one can afford to.
example: The tiny fire in Bob’s office makes Scrooge’s miserly habits visible in a way that a figure in an account book could not.

definition: Suggesting that something threatening is about to happen.
example: The bell that starts moving in Scrooge’s room is ominous because it rings without anyone touching it.

definition: So harsh or controlling that people lose freedom or hope.
example: The threat of losing his job makes Bob’s workplace oppressive, since even asking for another shovel of coal carries a risk.

definition: Willing to listen to an idea or learn from an experience.
example: By the time the last Spirit appears, Scrooge is receptive enough to ask for guidance even though he fears what he will see.

definition: Feeling deep regret for harm one has caused.
example: Marley is remorseful because he can now see the suffering he once had the freedom to relieve.

definition: Able to carry on or recover when life is difficult.
example: The Cratchits are resilient in the vision of grief, finding ways to comfort Bob even as each child misses Tiny Tim.

definition: Inclined to doubt something until there is convincing evidence.
example: Scrooge remains sceptical when Marley first appears, testing a frightening sight against the ordinary possibility of a bad supper.

definition: Serious and thoughtful in a way that suits an important moment.
example: The last Spirit’s solemn silence makes Scrooge supply the questions that he has avoided asking himself.

definition: A story in which people or events also stand for wider ideas.
example: The episode with Ignorance and Want works as an allegory because each child gives a social problem a human face.

definition: A brief reference to a story, person or event the reader may recognise.
example: The narrator’s allusion to the ghost in Hamlet prepares readers for a dead man’s return.

definition: A pattern in which the ending returns to a detail or situation from the beginning.
example: Bob and Scrooge meet in the same office again in the final stave. This cyclical structure lets us measure the change in their relationship.

definition: A character whose differences bring out qualities in another character.
example: Fred acts as a foil to his uncle when he greets Bob warmly on his way out of the counting-house.

definition: The placing of two details or scenes close together so the reader notices a connection or difference.
example: The juxtaposition of the Spirit’s feast and the hungry children beneath his robe makes their deprivation harder to ignore.

definition: A detail, image or idea that keeps returning and gathers meaning.
example: Fire is a motif that links kindness to Bob’s working conditions, from his tiny flame to Scrooge’s promise of more coal.

definition: A quality in a scene that makes the reader feel pity or sorrow.
example: There is pathos in Bob trying to speak steadily about Tiny Tim’s grave while his family listen.

definition: A group of words connected by a topic or idea.
example: The keys, padlocks and ledgers form a semantic field of business and security that makes Marley a prisoner of his old priorities.

definition: In a Victorian home, a large vessel used for heating water or boiling things.
example: The Cratchits boil their pudding in the copper, bringing the work of a wash-house into their Christmas feast.

definition: A length of cloth tied around the neck and worn with a shirt.
example: Scrooge takes off his cravat and puts on his nightcap before Marley appears, so the haunting interrupts a familiar bedtime routine.

definition: A British coin worth two shillings and sixpence in the money of Dickens’s day.
example: Scrooge offers the boy half-a-crown for a quick return with the poulterer’s man, turning an errand into a chance to be generous.

definition: Someone who makes or sells hats, especially women’s hats.
example: As an apprentice to a milliner, Martha works long hours, which helps explain why Christmas morning offers a rare chance to rest.

definition: The system of laws that organised relief for poor people and their families in England and Wales.
example: Scrooge invokes the Poor Law to justify refusing a donation, as though paying for public institutions settled what he owed his neighbours.

definition: A trader who sells birds such as chickens, geese and turkeys for food.
example: Scrooge sends the boy to the poulterer for the turkey, which gives him a way to help the Cratchits before he finds the words to speak to Bob.

definition: A verse of a song or poem, used by Dickens as the name for a chapter.
example: Calling each chapter a stave extends the musical idea in the title and invites us to read the five parts as one carol.

definition: In this setting, a large wheel that prisoners were forced to turn by stepping on it repeatedly.
example: Scrooge mentions the treadmill when asked to help the poor, revealing how closely he links need with punishment.

definition: Driven by a strong desire to gain more money or possessions.
example: Belle remembers a time before Scrooge became avaricious, which suggests that his greed grew out of choices he once could have made differently.

definition: Genuinely sorry for a wrong one has done.
example: Scrooge is contrite when he meets the charity collector again. He asks to be forgiven before whispering the size of his donation.

definition: Friendly and lively in a way that makes people enjoy being together.
example: Fezziwig makes the warehouse convivial by clearing space for dancing where his apprentices usually work.

definition: Eager to acquire or keep things for oneself.
example: Dickens introduces Scrooge as covetous before we see him with a single coin, so we first encounter greed as a habit of mind.

definition: Sorry for past wrongdoing and willing to put it right.
example: A penitent Scrooge approaches the charity collector he once dismissed and offers to make up for years of missed donations.

definition: Insecure and liable to be lost or made worse.
example: The couple who owe Scrooge money are relieved by his death because even a short delay in repayment matters to their precarious household.
